candidate.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide preventive teaching for chronic-disease self-care and behaviors that reduce injury and complication risk
candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — diabetic callus and footwear self-care teaching
candidate.educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic loss of protective sensation to avoid self-cutting calluses and use appropriately fitted pressure-reducing footwear with professional foot-care evaluation when risk lesions are present.

options.A: Avoid self-cutting the callus and arrange appropriate foot-care evaluation; footwear should fit properly and reduce pressure on high-risk areas.
options.B: Trim the callus with a sharp blade after soaking the foot because reduced sensation makes the procedure less painful.
options.C: Continue the tight shoes because pressure on a callus protects the skin underneath from ulceration.
options.D: Ignore the callus unless it becomes painful because loss of protective sensation makes painless lesions low risk.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care identify preulcerative corns and calluses, loss of protective sensation, and foot deformity as risk factors for ulceration. ADA preventive guidance advises against self-care of calluses and emphasizes appropriate footwear; people at increased plantar pressure or high risk may need customized pressure-relieving or specialized therapeutic footwear and foot-care specialist involvement. B risks injury to insensate skin. C can increase pressure and tissue damage. D is unsafe because neuropathy can make clinically important injury painless.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Loss of protective sensation and callus increase diabetic foot-ulcer risk; clients should avoid self-treatment of calluses and use appropriate footwear/foot-care support to reduce pressure and injury risk.
candidate.source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
candidate.source_locator: Foot Care — risk factors include LOPS and preulcerative corns/calluses; Recommendation 12.31 therapeutic footwear for high-risk individuals including LOPS/callus; Foot Care Education/Treatment — discuss appropriate footwear and no barefoot walking; initial management includes avoidance of self-care of ingrown nails and calluses and pressure-relieving footwear for increased plantar pressures
candidate.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
candidate.stem: A client with diabetes and loss of protective sensation has a thick plantar callus and says, “I’ll trim it myself with a blade and keep wearing my usual tight shoes.” Which response by the nurse is best?
